source.title: Hybridised Loss Functions for Improved Neural Network Generalisation
source.authors: Matthew C. Dickson; Anna Sergeevna Bosman; K. Malan

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether changing the loss function changes held-out accuracy, a generalization-related factor outside the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports test accuracy for nine loss-function variants on five datasets. It does not test random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, convolutional versus fully connected architectures, optimizer comparisons, batch-size effects, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples.
record.test_reason: The study compares loss functions in small feedforward classifiers. None of V1–V8 is tested. Sharp minima are invoked as a possible explanation using prior literature, without measuring sharpness or its association with generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' conclusion: hybridization improved generalization across the five problems, and reactive SE-to-CE switching was best on average or statistically indistinguishable from the best. This is an overall conclusion, not evidence that every hybrid improved on both baselines; on Cancer, CE alone was also among the best.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares loss-function variants, including staged and weighted hybrids; it does not reproduce the claim's random-label memorization or any listed version's intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and loss-function variant; the authors also report greater test-accuracy variability for some CE-containing variants on Fashion-MNIST.

fits_no_version.finding: Reactive SE-to-CE switching achieved the highest mean test accuracy on Glass, Diabetes, MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. On Cancer it was statistically tied with the best, including CE alone. Individual hybrids did not uniformly beat both baselines.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Combining or switching squared-error and cross-entropy losses can improve held-out accuracy in small single-hidden-layer classifiers trained with Adam.

record.problems: Only five datasets and small, single-hidden-layer ANNs were tested; the authors say the networks were selected to be minimally sized. No training-error values are reported alongside test accuracy, so the train-test gap cannot be compared. The reported MNIST CE25 SE75 table value 0.09292 conflicts with the surrounding prose describing the hybrid results; retained exactly as printed.

untested.parts: No fixed random-label fitting or natural-versus-random-label held-out comparison.
No width sweep, zero-training-error threshold, or post-interpolation test-error comparison.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
All experiments use Adam; no optimizer comparison. Switching losses does not test switching optimizers.
No within-workload batch-size comparison or large-batch training-recipe intervention.
No dropout comparison. Speculation about inactive ReLU neurons does not test dropout.
No magnitude-aware perturbation measure, generalization-gap ranking, or comparison against norm and margin measures.
No memorization estimation or removal-and-retraining experiment.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T2 classification mistakes a new generalization-related intervention for a test of a listed version. Discussion of narrow minima and a citation to Keskar et al. do not establish V5 or V7. All states remain cannot_determine relative to V1–V8, rather than absent.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of train and test accuracy for natural versus random labels.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
Adam is used throughout; no adaptive-versus-SGD comparison or optimizer tuning comparison.
Batch size is set by dataset; no batch-size comparison or fixed-epoch large-batch penalty test.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or comparison of generalization-gap measures.
